blocks.x: JOSEPH VERNON "BIG JOE" TURNER JAZZ ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPTION
Patricia Willard, Interviewer
Reel One
Los Angeles, California
Reel 1
May 7, 1980, and this is the Oral History with Joe Turner. Joe, your full name, I read in The Encyclopedia of Jazz, is Joseph Vernon Turner. Is that right?
That's right.
And when were you born?
May the eighteenth, 1911.
So we're doing this right before your birthday.
Yeah, I'll have a birthday comin' up this month.
Good. And you were born in Kansas City?
Born in Kansas City, Missouri.
Mnnn hmmmmm, and you lived there for quite a few years, right?
Yeah, I lived there about eighteen or nineteen years.
And you started singing when you were just a child. Is that right?

I started out to singin' when I was about thirteen years old. I picked it up, singin' in school, and me an' the kids used to have a little quartet...used to sing for our own pleasure, and after that, I moved up to listen to my uncle play the piano in the hall wh've lived at. He worked at a nightclub, and he used to come by every day and play the piano. When there were some new songs would come out, he come by and let me...and play 'em for me...and learn 'em to me. So I was singin' pop and jazz songs 'way before I started singin' the blues.
Ohhh, what was your uncle's name?
Uncle Charlie.
His last name?
Reel 1
Bryant. Charlie Bryan.
B-R-Y-A-N, Bryan?
That's right.
And where was it that he worked?
He worked at a nightclub down Independence Avenue.
Do you remember the name of the nightclub?
No. We call it Backbiters Club. Jab Stone used to run it. A fellow called Jab Stone. He used to wear a twenty-dollar goldpiece on his watchchain.
That sounds like a line from a blues I've heard.
Yeeahhh. He was real cool. Real friendly person.
How old were you when you got to know him?

Well, I had another brother-in-law who worked there as a bouncer--checked the door when people come in--so I used to go down there with my other friend, and he used to be down there in the daytime, fooling around. So they had paint on the windows so you couldn't see in. So we used to go down there--me and a bunch of kids--and play in the joint with some razor blades, and we'd take the razor blades and shave off the paint on the inside so we could peep in at night. So that's what we used to do. And I watched people dance there and havin' their fun, and I always said, "When I grow up, I want to get in there and do my number." So I used to go down there every night. They start about nine o'clock, so I didn't have to go to bed about ten...ten thirty, so we... bunch of kids used to run down there and be in front of the joint. They run us off, you know: "Where you all kids doin' down here? You ought to be home in bed."
Reel 1
We wait till the man go back inside, then we come back out. Then we can come right back and peep in through the holes we done scratched in there.
Was there a law that said you had to be a certain age before you could go into a nightclub?

Oh, yeah, you had to be twenty-one. And...we nothin' but kids, though. We's a long ways from twenty-one. So that club lasted a long time, and I can remember when I got to be of some age, a little bigger there--fifteen...sixteen years old--they closed up. So used to be a lot of nightclubs on Independence Avenue--all kinds--honky tonks--nice, up-to-date joints...'course the I-talians used to run 'em. They were back in the days when the I-talians live on one side of town, and the Negroes live on the other. 'Cause they had all kinds of people down on the Avenue...Chinamans...Jews...gentiles...every kind of people that you would could think of, and they had stores--second-hand stores and restaurants and things like that. So we used to run errands for the people who worked in them stores and things. Had an ice cream parlor on the corner. It sold nickel ice cream cones so we hustle out and get the people give us a dime or a nickel so we could buy an ice cream cone. We used to have a lot of fun. We used to go junkin' all the time. We'd go hustle up bottles, bones and stuff like that. We take 'em to the junkyard. The junkyear give us maybe fourteen or fifteem cents. But that was good money then. We hustling 'em up a storm.
Bones, too?

Yeah, you buy bones, bottles, rags and iron, copper ...stuff like that. One time I saw a whole dead horse in the junkyard. I couldn't figure that out. 'Course, was a law that wasn't too strict then so the fellow in the junkyard got by with it.
Reel 1
I wonder what he would do with the dead horse.
They use the bones.
For what?

They sell the bones, and they make glue out of them. And you could buy...you could take any kind of junk down there and get ten ...twelve cents. You could hustle milk bottles--things like that. Go by, and if you have some bottles settin' on the porch...we swipe 'em. Soda pop bottles--that was a...that was a daily thing, hustlin' up soda pop bottles...old rags and things people throw away. We could go by there and take a... We didn't have too much to weigh, we put a rock in there--wrap it up in the rags, and the Jew used to catch us. He say this too heavy for a bunch of rags, and he'd look in the bag. Don't look in the bag. That ain't kosher. Don't look in the bag. He'd take the rocks out, then weigh 'em. Try to pull the wool over his eyes but we weren't too slick. He know that bag o' rags didn't weigh that much. And then, we used to hustle around, go to the different nightclubs...in the daytime because they wasn't closed in the daytime. The janitor'd be in there. We'd go down and know everybody...we knowed everybody on the Avenue anyway. We knowed all the people worked in there so we used to go down there, see whether we could do the same thing to they joints--scrape the paint off the...the windows. Some of them didn't have no windows so we used to go 'round to the back and raise a window...go inside and raise a window so we could see in there at night in the bathroom...see what was goin' on. Used to have a lot of the gimmicks we would pull. We used to go...when we would go to school...went to school...I went to Lincoln School...was on...I don't remember the street it was on now, it's been so long ago, and we used to go there in the Maytime and wrap the Maypole, pledge allegiance
Reel 1

to the American flag...all that jazz. And we used to play ball in the back of the school, and it wasn't too big a yard so we hit the ball, and we'd break the window, and everybody would scatter. Jus' know the teacher gonna raise some sand 'n! "Who did that?" and tell us, "Go out in the alley and play with the ball. Don't play it in the schoolgrounds...gonna break out the windows." But we didn't pay no attention. We'd go right on back and do the same thing the next day.
We used to go out on a corner at night, sit around on the...in the park and sing. We had a quartet. We sing up a storm.
Remember any of the songs?
Huh?
Remember any of those songs that you sang?

Oh, they was old spiritual songs we used to sing, and...uh...which we'd heard in church or heard on the wind-up Victrolas. We used to do all that kind of jazz. We had a lot of fun. We took our time in the daytime when we wasn't in school. We get out of school, we all hang out on the corner and watch the kids fight and act a fool, and there'd always be a big gang of them, always something went all wrong... kid be fightin' up and down the street. I never was a fighter, so I be the onlooker, and used to go back and forth to church. They would a had to go to church during the week. Mother took us to church...all the club meetings and to church we went. On Sunday we went, and the preacher had 'bout five or six children, and one of them was a piano player, a girl, so she used to get together in the daytime when we weren't in school. We'd go round there in church and play the piano. We be singing everything...
Reel 1

in the church...and the people say, "Get them bad kids out of here. They ain't...they don't know nothin' about the Lord...the devil gonna get 'em." So then we start in playin' hymns, and the girl start playin' a hymn...a church hymn. We sang. They thought that was outa sight. An'll now they gettin' around to doin' somethin' right...once in a chain.

'Cause I didn't live but two...three blocks from the church. Church was on Charlotte--a street called Charlotte--[ ] Charlotte. I live about two...three blocks up the street in a big old flat. I fell down them steps for many a day. And I used to be crazy about dogs. So a man had a bunch of spitz dogs. He raised them. So I used to go up there and help him feed 'em. So he told me one day he gonna give me a dog. He finally got around to it. He give me a nice little puppy. I live on the third floor in the flat so while I hadn't got out of bed that mornin', my mom let the dog out on the porch. It fell off the porch and killed itself. I cried like a baby. That was the first little pet I ever had, and I thought that the world and all of that little dog.

And then we used to have...they used to have fish suppers, and people give rent parties and it...on a weekend, so they serve hot fish ...chicken...stuff like that. So my brother-in-law, he played the piano so he used to bring it along with him sometimes. A lady used to have a place like that. She was a...always...she had a son was sickly so she let me come and play with him all the time. So when they had a fish Friday an' Saturday night, I be in a...we be in upstairs room with her son, an' we just sit on the steps and listen...and watch the people dance and listen to the music.
Reel 1

So I...uh...my...a friend of mine, Uncle Charlie--I call him Uncle Charlie--he played the piano...he would always teach me different songs, like I said before, so sometimes I'd go down there and, "Play and let me sing."
Say, "You better get back up on them steps."
So, he used to let me...
Say, "Come on. You can sing one. Cain't stay down here long ...too long now."
So he let me sing up a storm. The people like to hear me sing. So it got to be a regular routine there so I learned how to sing, singing at fish fries, house rent parties and stuff like that.
By then, what kind of songs were you singing? Were you singing...is that when you were singing jazz, or were you singing the blues by then?
I was singing jazz. I was singing all the songs that they had out popular.
What...can you remember what songs?

I used to remember they had a fellow called Clarence Rand. That was before Bing Crosby's time, and he used to had a theme song, and I used to like the way he sing his theme song so I learned it. But now it slips my mind what the name of it was. And I used to listen to the radio and listen to all that music on the radio, and we had a wind-up Victrola at my house, and we had some records of all the old-time singers and stuff, and one record that I liked was Ethel Waters. She was singing on a record, "Shoo Shoo Boogie Boo, I'm sick and tired of you. Find your place behind the moon..." So I liked that, so I used to
Reel 1

always get together with the boys and learn the words, and we'd sing it. We have a good time. We had a big park we used to go play in and right by the boulevard, and we used to sit there and count the cars go by, and we'd stamp 'em and pick out the Ford, the Chevrolet. What cars we know we could pick 'em off, and we sit there and have fun stampin' them. See who could get the most stamps--how many cars went by.
When you say, "Stampin' them," is that when you put your finger in your mouth, put it on your hand and go like that with your fist?

Yeah. Yeahh. So we had a lot of fun thataway. And we had a coupla cats in the gang that loved to fight so when one gang would beat up the other, we'd have us a ball, throwin' rocks at one another an' raisin' sand and like the kids're doin' today. We done that years ago. Then, the ones that go to different schools, when they play ball, whoever lost, we beat 'em up. The kids 'n' they be fightin' up and down the streets, on the ballpark, raisin' sand. All that stuff was when we was children.

And I used to go 'round and help blind people. We'd go pass the hat for the blind...so my mother was looking for me everywhere. One day...so a blind man came by, playing a guitar. So he stopped, played a few tunes, and he would pass the...pass his cup. So I took it upon myself to help pass the cup 'cause he couldn't see, and the people who lived... settin' on the porch 'n' everything...he couldn't get up there, so I take his cup and go pass the cup up to the people that's sittin' on the porch. So he got so he come by there every other day and pick me up, and we'd go all over town [ ] up and down every street. My mother didn't
Reel 1

know where I was. She goin' crazy lookin' for me. I didn't have no hat on or no shoes. So we used to...I used to go walk...holdin' his hand... walk him up and down the street. He had a cane. Only a lot of the people had dogs lead 'em but he didn't have no dog, and we used to go up and down the street, pass, go in all the stores 'n' joints 'n' things, pass the cup so we could get him some money so he played the guitar and sang for awhile. I picked up with him out there so he play something so I can sing. We sang. So I used to go around, lead him, and he'd play the guitar, and I'd sing, so that was a big kick for me.
How old were you then when you were doin' that?
Oh, I was about twelve years old.
When you were goin' out around with him, were you... was that when you were supposed to be in school?
Oh, it be on a weekend. Sometime we come by there, my mother send me to school. I never went to school too good. I didn't learn too much at school...'cause I was too playful, I guess. Now I miss it.
Do you remember the guitar player's name?
No, I don't remember his name. It's been years ago. I don't know if...I'd never remember his name.
How long did you do that with him--go out around town?

He used to come get me every weekend. That's when my mother found out where I was. She wouldn't let me go. After she found out what I was doin' and she decided it was all right, and on a weekend, he'd come by the house, and I'd get him by the arm, and we'd take off...
Reel 1
barefooted...no hat on...walk all through the hot sun all day long, beggin' for him.
Did you learn any new songs from him that you didn't know before?

I...the songs he sing I never heard before so I didn't bother about 'em. He was singin' that old-time folk songs, and funny I never picked up on none of them. I was so busy worrying about my own self 'cause I learned all my singing off of records.
What was the first blues...the first time you remember hearing the blues?

Well, my Uncle Charlie used to play the blues all the time on the piano so when he come by...we had the piano in the hall there...he would come by and play the piano for us. Everybody would be sittin' around drinkin' home brew, and livin' it up, so it was...the piano was out in the hall, so they had a bunch of apartments there. So the people used to come out in the hall with they home brew and listen to the music. Was a bunch of elderly people there...had about all the fun they could have. So my Uncle Charlie--he come by there and play for the elderly folks. He used to do it about every other day or so. He always come by to see us, to see my momma and my sister and the kids in the neighborhood.

So I used to...had a man had a coupla horses and a wagon...he used to haul stuff around in it, and sometime I'd get on the wagon and ride with him and go 'round and pick up junk...stuff like that. And if anybody wanted to move, we'd move them in his wagon. So I learnt...every once in awhile, I used to let him...he used to let me drive a little bit, you know. I thought that was big kicks. Drivin' two horses. Didn't have to pay me nothin'. Just let me ride and drive the horses. So he had a barn in the
Reel 1

back of the place that we lived at, where he kept his horses at, so I used to go down there and when he hitch 'em up, get a wagon. I would help him. So I learned how to hitch up the horses and the wagon by myself, so one day I decided that I was gonna take the wagon out myself. So I hitched up the horses, hitched them to the wagon, and off I took. Got all the kids, put 'em in the wagon...we ridin' around havin' a ball. And the man was goin' crazy lookin' for his horses and the wagon. He didn't know what happened to them. We rode around for two...three hours. Everybody was lookin' for the man's wagon. So finally we came back with it. He was so glad to see us. My momma like to beat the devil out of me for runnin' off with the man's wagon and horses 'cause she wasn't scared I'd get hurt.

So I...uh...used to be a place up the street a few blocks where they sold horses at--a regular auction place. So I used to go up there and hang around on the weekends...on Saturday when they have the auction. So you get a quarter if you lead the horse out, you know. So I was so little and skinny...heaven look at me now. Don't nobody believe that I weighed about ninety pounds. So I would ask the people up there, "Let me make a quarter. Let me lead your horse."
Say, "Get away, kid. You get killed. This horse is a bad horse. You can't lead him."
"Oh, yes I can. Just gimme...just gimme the quarter. I'll bring him around. I'll lead him around."
So some of the fellows said, "Okay. Okay, kid. All right."

So I have to lead the horses around, goin' in a circle, lead 'em around. People bid on the horses, you know. So, I got so that I got real slick on doin' that. So my friend...where I used to go over to his
Reel 1

house all the time and listen to his Friday and Saturday night fish fries and listen to the piano and sing but I... But his mother would buy him anything 'cause he was real sickly, and I pumped it into his head...I said, "Get your mother to buy us a horse and wagon so we can go out and hustle. Get some junk like everybody else doin'."

So he asked his mother to get him a horse and wagon, and so she did. She got a big old white horse an' a wagon, and we used to get on that wagon and go junk up barrels and trash and all that stuff. We used to go all downtown, picking up boxes 'n' things, take 'em to the junkyard. And I learned how to hustle--me and him--thataway. So finally, while we was drivin' the horse and wagon, we got an idea--ice man used to come along...man that sell ice and coal in a wagon--so I tol' him that we oughta go in the ice business. We could make us some money. We get rich. So's we didn't have no customers. Well, I mean, we jus' go out and holler up and down the street: "Ice."

So his mother went and bought us some ice, so we got a coupla cakes o' ice. We didn't know how to cut it. We had a ice pick an' things like that but we didn't know...we didn't know the skill of cuttin' it, you know. So if you was to say, "Gimme a twenty-five pounds of ice," we didn't know how to cut the ice in, say, twenty-five pounds or what, so we just chip off a big hunk.

So the people got slick then: Where these kids don't know what they doin' so they buy ice from us because we give them more than they supposed to git, you know. We'd make us about a dollar off a cake o' ice. We thought we made...we thought we gettin' rich.
And then we had a lot of toys that he had, so when... I always wanted to play the drums. I don't know where I got that from but I
Reel 1

always wanted to play the drums. When I see the cat in the nightclub when I peep through the window, playing the drums, I thought I would like it to have something to beat on, so I had to go home and get all my momma's pans and stuff and beat all one of them. I beat the pans until the stuff would pop off of the pan and be beatin' 'em on with two sticks out of a chair. I be makin' some noise.
"Will you stop that kid makin' all that noise beatin' on them tin pans!"
I say, "These ain't no tin pans. I'm playin' the drums. I'm gonna be a drummer."
So we had a lotta fun doin' that.

Then I had another fellow was sick...had a t.b. So he was a beautiful piano player. He could play a piano like nobody's business. Oh, when they let him out of the hospital, he come home and stay awhile. So I used to go down to where he lived at, and he'd play the piano for me, and we had a lot of fun thataway. And that's why I was pickin' up on some more music. But he was a terrific piano player. He didn't live too long but I remember him.
You remember his name?

No, I can't remember that man's name, Charlie... not Charlie. Willie somethin'. I think his name is Willie Bryant or something like that. An' we used to have plenty of fun, jus' me and him, we were settin' up an' he play the piano for me and play all the popular numbers. And then I learned how to sing the popular songs...pop songs...was on the ...on the radio and on the Victrolas. So I picked up some more education that way by singing. 'Course I never did have a idea that I was gonna be
Reel 1
a singer.
What did you think you were gonna be?

A drummer. I just loved to beat on things. I thought I was real good, beatin' on the pots and pans, knockin' all the bark off of... Then I finally left that alone, and I finally got interested in singing. 'Course I still didn't know I was going to try to be a singer. I just liked...that was something that I liked to do. 'Cause the only thing I got a good grade in in school was singin'. I'd sing up a storm-- all the school songs...stuff we singin' in school. You could hear my voice-- it was loud anyway--over all the kids.

And after that, used to love to play baseball. Tell you about breakin' out all the windows in the school. So they got so we go play ball in the park. So it was on...was on...between two streets. Wasn't a very big park. Had a lot of vines and bushes and things. Street's still there in Kansas City, called Paseo. Used to have a lot of houses...big flats, all up and down the side of the streets.

I went back there after three or four years ago...four or five years ago maybe, and they was tearin'...tore down all them places. Me-- I don't know why I expected it to look like it did when I was a kid but that was just somethin' I had in my mind. And it kinda made me feel bad to see all them tearin' down all them old places 'cause they been there for years. They need to tear 'em down.

And then I picked up [ ] gettin' a little older, still tryin' to sing. So then I started workin' for a bunch of I-talians. We didn't call them I-talians. We called 'em dagos. So they was all up and down the Avenue, too. So that was before Prohibition. But liquor went out when I was a kid. Used to have saloons, and they, uh... My mother
Reel 1

and a bunch of her friends used to...they didn't allow women in saloons so they'd get somebody to go down there and get them a big bucket of beer. So they'd have a ball. They be sittin' on the porch drinkin' beer, playin' the old Victrola. I set around and watch 'em. I thought they was all crazy...out there dancin' and havin' a ball and drinkin' beer on the porch. Cut it [the tape recorder] off a minute.

After we done all those things, I begin to grow older and I suddenly got the idea that I wasn't gonna be no drummer 'cause I couldn't ...I had two left feet. Don't one foot as good as the other. You need two good feet to be a drummer. Two good hands, too. So I could beat the drum with one foot, couldn't beat the cymbal with the other one. Why I should ...an' after all that, I got so I'd go down to the clubs in the daytime and people leave their drums in there, so...

A friend of mine later on married my sister. He was Charlie's brother, and said he was the night man on the door. I went down there and clean up the joint in the daytime. I had a chance to get in there an' see what was happenin'. 'Course, a lookin' through the windows, could see the bartenders, you know, servin' people drinks over the bar so I got a idea that that was a good profession to be in. So I got into that. I wanted to be a bartender. So I tried. I wasn't old enough to get behind nobody's bar 'cause... This was after they had Prohibition. When I grow up, I was a pretty good-sized kid, there, when [ ] liquor and beer and stuff.
So then I started workin' in nightclubs, and I worked for a bunch of I-talians.
How old were you when you started workin' in the nightclubs?
Reel 1
I was about sixteen...seventeen years old.
How tall were you?
I was about as tall as I am now...almost.
Now, what are you? About six, three?
I'm six, one-and-a-half. [ ]

I was big for my size so I used to go around... To get in the nightclub, I had to dress up like a grown person. My mother used to dress me in Buster Brown things and stuff like that. So I would get so I'd go and get my grandfather's long pants and roll 'em up and get some eyebrow pencil, make me some mustache, put on...put on my grandfather's clothes. They swallow me up but I still was dressin' like a man, and I would go sneak into the club when my brother-in-law wasn't on the door. They nailed me so they let me...I told them I was lookin' for him, so they'd let me...the man that was on the door would let me in.
So I'd go around and bug everybody, so they found out I was in there and they throw me out. So I used to go 'round and bug everybody ...listen to the music...let me sing, let me sing.
"What're you doin' here, kid? You cain't sing. You get outa here." Say, "What're you doin' with all them clothes on like that? You ain't got no business in here. You too young."
Say, "I'm old enough to be in here. Don't tell me that. I'm old enough to be in here. A lot of people in here ain't as old as me," I tell 'em, you know.
They thought I was a baaad boy. So I learnt how to get by with that. I get by with it every so often. But somebody know me come in there and tell me to hit them...I'd have to hit 'em.
Reel 1
"You gotta get outa here. You too young to be in here. You momma don't know you down here."

So I get kicked out but I never gave up. I used to go back down to the clubs. So after I started workin' with the I-talians, I was ... Tendin' to help the lady washin' the glass. I wasn't tendin' no bar. A friend of mine, y'know I knew, she used to be a barmaid, so I knew her, so she let me come in there.
"I want to see Jessie."
Her name was Jessie.
"I got a message for her...from her momma."

So the man on the door let me in. So I go in there and talk to Jessie. Thought she put me... She set me on a chair an' set me beside the bar. Now, if you set there, you could listen to the music awhile afore you gotta go home. [Coughs.] Boy, she was a bit older than me, so...she's a very pretty girl, too. So that helped a lot. So she was a barmaid. So while she's tendin' bar an' everything, I'd sit there and listen to the music. When she get busy, I'd sneak over to the bandstand:
"Let me sing. Let me sing."
"Get outa here. You cain't sing."
They would throw me out all the time.
Say, "Yes, I can."

I told 'em my Uncle Charlie taught me how to sing. So everybody know Uncle Charlie. All the musicians did. He was a piano player in another place down the street. So...after I'd bugged everybody around there, I got so...I don't care nothin' about goin' to nightclubs. I just go on about my business.
Reel 1

So I got me a job sellin' papers. I used to go...got me a little paper route, and on the evenings they had them little...on weekends, they had them little [envelope ??] papers, you know, they'd put around in different places, where it was goin' on, all the entertainers and who sang there and all that stuff, so I got a job deliverin' them so that got me back in the nightclubs, so I would...when I bring 'em they papers and stuff, I look the joint over and see what I could see...see what's goin' on. 'Course it be in the daytime. Wasn't nothin' happenin' too much in the daytime. Few stragglers sittin' around the bar, drinkin' beer.

So, I kept on that for a good while, and then I picked up on...well, I said, "Now, this close as I'm ever gonna get. If I wanna be anybody, I better get...I gotta get in here in the nighttime." So I went and jumped into my grandpa's clothes again. Tried it again. So my momma didn't know where I was at, so it be about nine or ten o'clock, and I would go and get a...get one of those...my little sticks that I had...I broke out a chair...told the man, "Let me play the drums. I'm a pretty good drummer." "You cain't play on my drums. You break 'em."

So I a real nuisance. So I went back after that, tried to get help on my schoolin'. Never was too good on goin' to school. I was a slow learner. My sister 'n' them...my sister was smart. She was way ahead of me 'cause she is four years older than me. She was so smart, and everybody thought I should keep up with her. I never did catch her in school. So when she wind up getting married, that was a horse of another color.

But, so then I started to workin' in a grocery store. I was a helpin' put up stuff in the store, and then I learnt with the stamp, a puttin' the prices on the stuff. So that did...that didn't last too long. It wasn't exciting enough. So I went right straight back to doing
Reel 1
what I was doing before...back, tryin' to get into nightclubs.

So I learnt by sittin' down listenin' to different people play and listen to 'em sing. Was a man called Slam Stewart who was a helluva piano player and could sing up a storm. So I finally started hanging out with him. So I run get his cigars for him, do little odd jobs, whatever he wanted, I was right there. I was his boy. So I could slip in anywhere he worked at.

He had a piano at his house, too. So I go by there in the daytime and listen to him play and sing. He be practicin'. He always have three or four people in his house. They be drinkin' beer, havin' a good time. So I listened to him play and sing for a long time, and then he used to play for me and let me sing. He said I could sing pretty good, so I used to try to sing like him.

All in the meantime, I was thinkin' of it all the time. I was thinkin' how I was gonna be get into the nightclub where he worked at 'cause I was gettin' a little older, so finally I got a chance to get into a nightclub where he worked at. I never will forget. It was on Independence Avenue and Truce. Upstairs. So I used to go up there and say, 'I want to see Mr. Slam Stewart. I got some cigars for him. I'm supposed to bring him his cigars.' So they let me by. I'd go in and bring him his cigars, and I'd ask him if I could stay awhile and listen to him play.
'Sit down right over there, son.'

So I sit there and listen to him play, watch the people dance, have a good time. I said, 'This is for me. This is what I want to do. This is somethin' I wanna do.' But I didn't know how to go about it.

So, finally, when I got out of school... I didn't get out. They kicked me out for bein' late all the time. I didn't show up at all. I'd go fishin'. Me and a bunch of the boys go down by the river and go swimmin', and a couple of us got drown'd down there. So that took kinda the sails outa my windpipe there. I didn't want to wind up like that... 'cause I couldn't swim that good but I had a lot of nerve. I would get out there with the rest of them that could swim. I follow them.

So, one day we swimmin' so we...the water wasn't too deep, and the place where we's at had a big island out in the middle of it, so the kids say, "We gonna swim out to the island." Big, old muddy river--the Missouri River. So, he say, "If you don' go, you're a...you're a scaredy cat. You can't be with the bunch if you don't come on in with us."

So I practically walked over there. I didn't swim 'cause I couldn't swim that good. It wasn't that deep right there. So we went over, and we got over on the island, and everybody decided after we got over there...played around on the island awhile, and we decided to go back. Well, they went back on the other side. Was deep over there. So, I tried, and my little swimmin' didn't do so good, so I like to got drown'd. So one of the kids got me out. An' I ain't gonna try that no more. I got scared...scared to go in the river again...'cause a coupla my friends got drown'd. Good little friend of mine, was a real tight buddy, used to sing in the quartet with us. He got drown'd. He went down and died down in the river and come up under a big boat, and he couldn't hold his wind long enough to get out from under it, so they...he got drown'd, and they fish around in the river there for him a couple of days, and they finally found him. We was down there every day...till they found him. His mother didn't

believe that he was in the river.
"Oh, yes he was. He went off in there."
So I got the devil beat out of me about that. My momma whipped my butt for goin' down there, jumpin' in the river, actin' the fool. But she didn't have to get on me too much. I was kinda leery. I was too scared to go back in there too much. But after that, a coupla kids got drownded, an' I said, "Oh, no. That ain't for me. If I never swim, I ain't gonna do that no more. I ain't gonna be that big a fool."
'Course I was a nice size boy then. I was gettin' older, and I begin to get interested in girls. So there used to be a little lady. She lived cross the street from me. I thought she's the prettiest thing I ever saw in my life. So I used to go to the store for her all the time. And finally she moved...her and her old man...moved in the flat where I was living at, in the front, so, her old man beat her up one time, so I saw her all beat up with a black eye and everything. I thought that was terrible thing I ever saw in my life, so I didn't dig him no more. He used to tell me to go to the store. I wouldn't go for him.
"No. I got somethin' to do. I ain't got time."
'Cause I didn't like the way he done her. So, after she got better, they were...her and my momma and a bunch of 'em was on the porch, drinkin' beer. So I decided that I was gonna taste the beer while they wasn't lookin'. So I got me a swallow out of my momma's glass. I didn't like it 'cause it was bitter. I couldn't dig that. So I said to myself, "What are you drinkin' that junk for? That ain't no good. Soda pop's better."
And then I thought of [

And then I go back to my friend's house that had the wagon and the horse. I say, "Well, let's go and hustle some more stuff...some more junk and stuff, and we gonna make us some money so we can buy us some ice cream cones!"

So we took the wagon. We took off. We had a policeman downtown used to directin' traffic all the time. Great, big tall man. He'd have to be about six...seven feet tall. "How you boys doin' today?"
"We ain't doin' so good. We ain't got no...we cain't find nobody throw no boxes out."
So he says, "Go 'round...go behind this store here. Try your luck."

So we went back there. It was a wholesale place, and they had a whole lot of boxes back there. We beat the...we got back there lucky and beat the old regular junkman come by and pick up the junk...we beat him back there, so we loaded up our wagon. We come back out. He let us by...hold up all the traffic...let us by. So we went off to the junkyard and get rid o' our paper boxes an' stuff. 'Cause we had to tear 'em up and tie 'em together. Wasn't nothin' too painful. We jus'...we went along to it, just like it wasn't nothin'. We'd be lucky to make thirty cents. That be a lot of money. Thirty cents. A whole wagonload of paper. So, when we got through junkin' and beatin' our heads against the bush, hustlin' up boxes and stuff, the little boy got sick, and he died, so I was scared of him, so his mother said she wanted the boys in the neighborhood to be the pallbearers. So she called over to my house, you know.
My momma told me, so I cried...'cause he was a good friend. And then...
How old was he?
Oh, I guess he's around fifteen...sixteen years old. And then, we...uh...my mother tried to talk me into goin' and bein' a pallbearer.
Say, "No, not me. I ain't gonna be no pallbearer." She say, "Well, it's your best friend. You ought to go." So, "I think it over."

So, afterward, I was...thought it over, and I told her, "Well, I talked myself into doin' it." So I went with the rest of the boys, and it wasn't too bad. We was his pallbearers. And, after that, the mother had the wagon, and the horse was [yamping ???] Would I come over there and work the horse out sometime? Or she gonna get rid of it.
I told her, "No, don't get rid of the horse and wagon. No, no, no. Don't do that."

So, she got so that she would let me come over there and hitch up the horse and wagon, and I got another buddy of mine. We go hustlin' with the horse and wagon. So I learned how to drive pretty good. I was
Reel 2

pretty good with horses...'cause I, in the meantime, my people...my kinfolk live up in the country, so in the summertime, my momma would send me up there. We'd go up in the country, have a ball, goin' huntin' and run everybody's horses crazy, tryin' to ride 'em. Every summer I used to go up there till I got to be about twenty-one years old. And then I got old enough where I could get into nightclubs. My mother want to send me up in the country; I didn't want to go. I want to get into the music business.

So I finally went up and stayed a couple of weeks an' tore 'bout to bug everybody to death, so finally I come back home. My mother asked me did I have a good time. I go, "Yeah, I had a ball. I had a good time, ridin' all the horses, goin' huntin' with the dog, runnin' up and down the meadows."
So I had an auntie. She...when I'd go visit...she had about ten children. She had a couple of girls. The rest of 'em was all boys. So I had a good time with them.

So after I got out of runnin' the back boys up there, I got so I say, well, my Uncle Charlie was still workin' in the nightclub. So I decided, I say, "Well, I gonna take up where I left off at. I'm gonna go to try to get back in them joints and sing some. So I used to put on ...Saturday night I'd take one little bath and everything, and...
Momma ask, "Where you goin'?" Say, "I'm goin' to a party. Some of the kids havin' a birth-day party."
So we go to the party. Party break up about ten...twelve o'clock. So's...everybody hadda go to bed. Me, I didn't go to bed.
Reel 2
I say, "I'm goin' out to see my uncle." So I would go back down to the nightclub, hang around the door with him, watchin' all the pretty girls come in an' all the hipcats, havin' a ball.
So, finally, I told my uncle...I say, "I'm gonna go up to the band and ask 'em let me sing a song or two."
He didn't know I could sing at all. He told me...said, "They ain't gonna let you sing. You can't have nobody messin' up. This ain't no play place. You can't go up there and goof off."
So I said, "I ain't gonna goof. I'm gonna sing."
So, say, "They ain't gonna let you."
So, I went up there. I asked the man to let me sing. He wouldn't. So I thought, "I know where I'll go. I'll go up to another nightclub I know...where Jessie worked there."
So when I went down there to see Jessie, she didn't work there no more. She done got moved up. She was the manager of the place. So I told her, I said, "Let me sing."
She say, "Well, now, if it was left up to me...but it's left up to the ownership."

So I said, "Okay, I'll go over and ast [sic] him." So I met my piano player that I used to work with so long--Pete Johnson. He was playin' there. Him and a cat called Merle...was a drummer, another cat called Piano Red...had another cat called Jones--Deacon Jones. But he used to try to preach. So he used to try to preach, and he was...he'd play in the band at night.
So we went by there. I used to go up and ask 'em to let me sing. So I would beg 'em so much and bugged 'em so finally, they...I got the
Reel 2

manager, Jessie, to give 'em some drinks, so this I-talian that run the place, he needed somebody to run and go get the whiskey...back to the stash. So, there another fellow workin' there, he was doin' that. So I got acquainted with him, and then we used to go...I used to go wit' him when he take the two pitchers to go back and get the whiskey. So I know right where the stash was at.

So, we go back there, and maybe we set down and talk a little while, and he would dip the pitchers in a big barrel of corn whiskey. Had some other whiskey there called Dago Red. It was better than the white whiskey. All of it was corn liquor but one of them was red and one of them was white. So we just sat out and sat out here.
"I'm gonna take a taste of this."
So the fellow says, "You can't drink outa the pitcher 'cause it'll strangle you. [ ]"
So I'd holler at him, "Okay, let me try."

So, sure enough, I drank outa the pitcher, and it strangled me, an' I throw up. Just a mouthful. I couldn't swallow it, it was so strong. The first time I ever drank any whiskey. So I said, "Oaaaaghh! I don't see what they think they so crazy about this stuff for. This stuff make you sick!"

So, somethin' happened to the fellow that was workin' there, who was runnin' the whiskey. He got married or sumpin'...he moved away. So I knew the I-talians that run the place good, so they give me the job. All I had to do was go get the whiskey when the bartender wanted it,
Reel 2
bring it back, set the pitcher up on the bar, and I was through till they needed some more. But, still, I'm still workin' on this singin' bit, so I asked the cat, "Let me sing" again.
So I kept buggin' him so much that he says, "Well, come on, you can try. You can sing. You can get up there and make a fool out of you...outa yourself. And us, too!"
Say, "No," so I gonna play "You Drivin' Me Crazy."

Never will forget it. I hadda learn all the words. So they played "You're Drivin' Me Crazy." So I started singing. People got up and started dancing. So I got through. I got a round o' applause. Then on, I was a singer.
I took my time, and I learnt different songs to sing and everything. I was really cool.
What was the name of that club?
The Backbiters Club. So George Stone had died, and the dago had took it over. I suppose he was workin' for them in the first place.
Is that the way it worked during Prohibition? They would bring in the whiskey just a pitcher at a time?
Yeah. Uh huh.
How far away did they keep the barrel of whiskey?
It be across the street. Hadda cross the street to go git it.
And didn't it...did you have to hide it some kind of way or just walk...?
Reel 2
Jus' walk right out across the street with the pitcher 'cause the...
The pitcher in your hand, and nobody'd...nobody would say anything.
No. Nobody would say nothin' but the policeman ...was gettin' paid off. They didn't bother you. Till one of...
But if they were being paid off, why keep it across the street? Couldn't they have just kept it...
No, they couldn't keep it in the joint...couldn't keep too much of it.
They still maybe could get raided?
They get raided every now and then because you had to make a showin', you know.
They didn't want to lose any...
They...they...they...every now and then they'd raid the joint.
Mmm. Hmmm.

You'd have to throw the whiskey out. Had a tub back there with a lot of Lysol in it, an' you throw it in the Lysol, and [ ] flashing lights. Had a man 'cross the street, one on each corner, who watched for the coppers, and when they see the coppers comin', he would flash the lights, so the lights would flash on and off in the joint, so they know the police was comin', so everybody would drink up their whiskey or throw it out, and so when the police come in, didn't make no difference to them no way because when they come, they was goin' to raid the joint anyway. Hadda raid it for a showin'. Hadda make it look good. They couldn't just let the joint...just raid one joint tonight
Reel 2
and maybe the next joint tomorrow night...different like that...just go down the line.
About how often did...was there a raid in one club?
Well, every now and then, they'd be two...three weeks at a time, so they would ride...uh, take you to jail, and they ride everybody down to jail...everybody in the paddy wagon.
Everybody who was in the place?
Yeah. Take 'em all, and you jus' go in there and sign your name, an' they let you right out.
You didn't have to pay a fine or anything?
No, the man who run the place get 'em all out. So that's the way they run it. All they used to say about "Ride down and walk back" because you didn't have no money to get a cab.
So bartending was just as popular a profession during Prohibition as it was when drinking was legal?

Oh, yeah. Yes, indeed. I got a friend right now in Kansas City who's still tendin' bar. His name's Jesse Fisher. We call him Kingfish. I saw him about four...five years ago when I was there. He was tendin' bar aroun'...he's the one who learned me how to tend bar. 'Course, wasn't much to it. You hadda know the different whiskeys--the red and the white--sell soda pop, draw beer. And they had a big time [ ] the name bartender. He mixed all the different drinks, so when he would be mixing drinks, I would watch him. So he found out what I was doin', so when he get ready to mix a drink, he turn his back on me so I couldn't learn but he couldn't keep his back turned all the time.
Reel 2

When he get crowded, he have to make 'em up in a hurry, so he'd mix a drink, and I watch him, what he put in it and everything, you know. I learned how to mix up drinks. Wasn't too bad then 'cause they didn't have too many bigtime drinks anyway. 'Course, then, in them days, it was a regular routine, goin' to work at nine o'clock, gettin' off at five o'clock in the mornin'. Joint be open all night long. Between times, the band would take a hour...a half an hour break. Then you had the gamblin' goin' on in the back o' the place. All the tips they'd made, they go back there and try to gamble. It was just like up in Las Vegas there. Silver dollars stacked up. Look like you got a million dollars there. Ain't nothin' but about two...three hundred dollars' worth of silver dollars. The man set aback behind there...had a stick man who rake up the dice... regular routine. That's the way they did it.

I was brought up in learnin' all that stuff 'cause I saw it when I was young, you know, so it wasn't nothin' new to me. And I took my time and learnt how to bartend so when the...when the entertainers wasn't workin', I'd go up and get behind the bar. I learned how to tend bar, and I git up, go on with my apron and everything on, I get up there and sing for the people. They's call me "The Singing Bartender." That's what they knowed me by...kept me busy. So that was a lot of fun because I always wanted to sing anyway, and I took my own good time. I was ...

In between times, when I wasn't runnin' whiskey...well, I didn't want to go back too often 'cause I'd take two good pitchers, and while they be serving them, I go take two more. Couldn't bring too much 'cause it would be a waste. Y'hear the police comin', you have to throw it out. So I always keep a couple extra pitchers sittin' on the side where I stood at.

I was...I was a bartender but I was just a'pourin' out straight drinks...stuff like that. I wasn't slick as the bigshot was, makin' all that mixed drinks and stuff. He was good at it, y'know. I was just learnin'. In the meantime, I'm runnin' back, gettin' the whiskey an' everything, an' I'm takin' care of business.
How much money would you make in doin' all that?
Ohhhh, make about fifteen...twenty dollars.
A week? Or a night?
No. A week. Wasn't makin' no money.
A week. Didja ever get tips?
I made a lotta...I made a lotta tips. I went... When I get up to sing, that's where I'd make the money, singin' off... makin' money off...people give me money to sing.
So you got paid fifteen or twenty dollars a week by the man you worked for.
Yeah.
And then you got tips on top of that when you sang.
Yeah. Made a lotta money singin'.
I would think so. I bet the people...

Didn't take a lot of money to live anyway. Had a good time. It was fun for me. It was all a big laugh. People who was serious about it didn't mean nothin' to me. It was just more fun for me, you know. I enjoy that. I took my own time, an' I was my own boss, an' I was all right with the head boss.

We used to have...we finally got a nightclub, and one of 'em had no liquor there. Back in the Prohibition days, we got a nightclub called The Cherry Blossom. No, it was The Suns... It was the Black and Tan. 'Cause we named it Black and Tan but it was a big furniture store on the corner of Independence Avenue and Charlotte.

So, somehow or other, the furniture store closed and moved out. So I told the dago boss that I know where to get him...to have a fabulous nightclub at, so he was lookin' around, say, he wanted a bigger place, so I say, I told him, I say, "I know where you get a bigger place at. Make a beautiful nightclub." There wasn't but about five or six blocks down the street but the dago ain't paid no attention to it.
Say, "Where..." He called me Daddy Long Legs. Say, "Where's it, Daddy Long Legs?"
I says, "Down the street."

So he got a...he had a Packard car, a big old Packard car-- even have a sireen on it...like the policemen's. So we get in the car, and we drive down there, and I showed it to him. I said, "That's the place. Right there." So, there was somebody in there, cleanin' up the place. So we went on in and looked it over. Say this would make a nice nightclub. It was what you call a real nightclub...this'd make a beautiful nightclub...was a great, big place, had a big balcony all 'round it. At the top, there's a big balcony. Down in the bottom...it was a huge place. So we say, "This is where it's at. We can put the white folks over here on one side of the balcony...and really have a nice nightclub. You know."
So we got so we finally took it over and opened it up. We call it The Black and Tan Nightclub. So the Black and Tan was on and runnin'.

So finally he got tired of me. He couldn't watch his bowl because me and Kingfish were behind the bar so he couldn't watch us all the time, so naturally, I would learn how to mix a drink outa...one of them walk up and ask for different names of drinks. He say, "You can't mix the drink. You don't know what you doin'."

"Yes, I do. Here try me."

And they name off the different funny names o' drinks. I'd mix it all up together...had the shaker and everything. I watch him an' I learn how. I'd shake it all up and measure it.

"Try that."

By then, how old were you?

Yeah.

I got so I'd go out on Twelfth Street. We used to have...we moved up to another flat when Momma was the manager of it, and we had a...always kept maybe one or two apartments empty. So, we got so a bunch of us fellows got together, and we had a...a joint. We sold whiskey. Bootleg whiskey. We sell it by the half-pint. Used to have a white fellow used to hang around with us. He was a printer...worked in a newspaper. He show up every month. When he get on his benders, he come by, sittin' around: "All you poor boys need a haircut!"
